title: Scheduler leader staleness — pending pods spike (scratchpad)
content:
Summary:

Loose notes from the on-call timeline investigating a large spike of Pending pods starting 2025-01-14 09:13 UTC that correlated with a temporary scheduling stall. Behavior observed: pending pods accumulated across clusters (prod-1, prod-2), scheduler leader reported high reconcile latencies, many predicate/equivalence-class checks became stale and scheduler restarted several times due to leader election churn.

Why this doc: scratchpad for artifacts, commands run, quick mitigation steps and follow-ups. Intentionally informal — will craft a proper postmortem after we validate root cause and fix plan.

High-level impact:
- ~1200 pods Pending across prod-1 over ~25 minutes (peak)
- Customer-facing latency for model endpoints increased (restarts, queued requests) but no data loss
- Autoscaler triggered scale-up repeatedly, but pods remained Pending (bind failed)

Timeline (rough):
- 09:11 UTC: alerts for pending-pod-count start firing (pager).
- 09:13 UTC: first on-call on pager (Lena) notices scheduler leader change; k-scheduler logs show leader-elect timeout errors.
- 09:15 UTC: multiple kube-scheduler replicas report long predicate computation (1000+ ms) and go into OOMKill/restart in prod-1.
- 09:18 UTC: control-plane monitoring (prometheus) shows spike in apiserver request latencies (List/Watches) from scheduler instances.
- 09:22 UTC: cluster-autoscaler launched scale-ups, nodes came up but pods remained Pending.
- 09:30 UTC: we temporarily scaled down scheduler replicas to 1 and restarted with --profiling to capture pprof; pending rate began to reduce as leader stabilized.
- 09:37 UTC: full recovery observed ~09:45 UTC after scheduler leader stabilized and kubelet NodeStatus updates resumed.

Key observations and hypotheses (working):
- Leader election churn seems central: multiple scheduler pods were flapping as leader due to heavy GC/blocking in scheduler main loop. That created windows where no stable leader was making binding decisions.
- Predicate/equivalence caches grew stale because the scheduler couldn't process watch events quickly (apiserver List/Watches lag).
- Some predicates that normally short-circuit were taking long (node affinity + custom webhook for node-label validation caused synchronous calls).
- Control-plane watch backlog: apiserver metrics show surge in request backlog — possibly due to longer-living watches from an unrelated component hitting etcd performance hiccup (etcd metrics show short raft heartbeat jitter around same time).
- Autoscaler more-or-less made the right reaction but binding requires a stable scheduler + fresh Node info. New nodes didn't appear in scheduler cache until leader re-established.

Commands and outputs captured (snippets):
- kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/kube-scheduler -l app=kube-scheduler --since=30m\  (looked for "failed to process" / "leader election" entries)
- Example log line: "I0114 09:14:02.123456 1 leaderelection.go:243] failed to renew lease: context deadline exceeded"
- prometheus query (apiserver): apiserver_request_latencies_summary{verb="LIST"} spike at 09:14-09:20
- kubectl get pods -A --field-selector status.phase=Pending | wc -l -> 1187 at peak

Quick mitigation (what we did during incident):
- Avoided mass restarts of scheduler replicas; coordinated a rolling restart with flags: added --bind-address=0.0.0.0 --use-legacy-policy-cache=false (experimental flag tweak) to reduce memory churn — this was a short-lived experiment and rolled back after validation.
- Temporarily disabled a custom mutating webhook that was doing synchronous node-label validation (linked in GH). This reduced per-predicate latency drastically.
- Increased lease duration for leader-election from 15s -> 30s temporarily to reduce leader churn while investigating.
- Restarted one of the etcd members after confirming healthy snapshots; this lowered raft heartbeat variance. (note: we coordinated with infra team.)

Root-cause (working hypothesis):
A combination of:
1) An expensive synchronous admission/mutation webhook called by the scheduler path (node validation) causing predicate evaluation to block on webhook response.
2) Short leader-election lease and transient GC pressure in scheduler process (memory spike due to policy cache growth) leading to frequent restarts and leader churn.
3) Minor etcd raft jitter causing apiserver watch/list latencies — exacerbated because scheduler replicas were consuming more CPU and memory, making them slower to renew leases.
These three together made a window where no stable scheduler instance could make binding decisions, so pending pods accumulated.

Why this was non-obvious: autoscaler and node provisioning were working, new nodes joined but scheduler cache didn't reflect NodeStatus quickly; typical ops path (scale up) looks like correct action but was ineffective when control-plane scheduling loop unavailable.

Evidence to collect for final postmortem (TODOs):
- pprof CPU and heap dumps from kube-scheduler instances around 09:13-09:25 (we started profiling at 09:30; need earlier samples if available).
- Full webhook latencies and traces from ingress of node-validation webhook (GH issue PR #45 references a change 3 days earlier).
- etcd raft heartbeat metrics and slow follower logs around timeframe.
- Apiserver watch/list tail logs and queue lengths.
- Autoscaler logs showing scale decisions (confirm no misconfiguration).

Immediate follow-ups (owners assigned):
- Priya: produce a conservatively-worded customer-facing incident summary (SL2/SL3 comms) and link to incident channel. (due 2025-01-18)
- Marcus: dig into webhook change PR (github.com/redwood-inference/scheduler-logs-PR/45) and produce latency histogram for last 7 days. Check retry/backoff. (due 2025-01-20)
- Ethan (me): reproduce leader-election churn locally with synthetic load and the webhook in the loop; test effects of leader-election lease tuning. (due 2025-01-21)
- SRE infra: schedule an etcd health check automation to run nightly, add alert for raft heartbeat jitter > 200ms over 3m. (request created: jira/ENGSRE-4123)
- Product/Platform: evaluate moving heavy validation from synchronous webhook to async admission check or background controller. (sync with product engineering, due 2025-02-02)

Permanent mitigations candidates (brainstorm):
- Move node-label validation to a lightweight gate inside kubelet or a background controller so scheduler path is not blocked.
- Increase default leader election lease (15s -> 30s) cluster-wide; or make it adaptive based on observed p99 reconcile latency.
- Harden scheduler memory usage: enable/optimize policy cache eviction and lower memory pressure via flag changes and targeted GC tuning.
- Add deeper observability around watch backlog: track watch queue length and expose a high-severity alert when watch backlog grows.
- Circuit-breaker for synchronous webhooks invoked during scheduling predicates (time out early and mark predicate as inconclusive rather than block).

Open questions / unresolved:
- Did a recent webhook change (PR 45) introduce an unexpected allocation pattern? Marcus to confirm.
- Could autoscaler be temporally delayed by the same watch backlog causing it to launch nodes too slowly? It looked fine but need logs.
- Any other control-plane components showing correlated GC spikes? apiserver & controller-manager metrics need deeper look.

Customer comms notes:
- No data loss, but slow provisioning and transient errors for customers of models during 09:13-09:45 UTC window. Recommended wording: apologize for degraded provisioning, summarize high-level cause (scheduler instability due to control-plane contention + webhook latency), and note mitigations + timeline. Priya to prepare draft.

Post-incident actions (short-term):
- Lock down webhook change PRs until telemetry + perf tests run in staging for 72h. (actioned)
- Add synthetic scheduling test to CI that includes our node-validation webhook (fail fast if predicate latency > 100ms p95).
- Add runbook entry: If pending-pods spike + scheduler leader churn observed -> check for synchronous webhook latencies, check kube-scheduler OOM/restart events, check etcd raft_broadcast jitter.

Runbook excerpt (draft):
- If pager fires for pending-pods > 300: 
  1) kubectl get pods -A --field-selector status.phase=Pending -o wide | head -n 50
  2) kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/kube-scheduler --since=15m | grep -E "leader election|failed to renew|failed to process"
  3) prometheus: alert -> query apiserver_request_latencies_summary & etcd_raft_proposal_duration_seconds
  4) Check mutating/admission webhook latencies: kubectl get --raw /metrics | grep webhook | sort -n
  5) If webhook latency high, temporarily set the webhook to "failurePolicy: Ignore" or scale webhook backend down for quick mitigation (coord with owning team)

Notes to self: preserve heap dumps and make sure we store pprof tarball in gs://redwood-infra-pprofs/2025-01-14-scheduler/ for postmortem. Also re-run the incident in staging with the webhook enabled to reproduce.

Appendix (raw snippets):
- scheduler log excerpt: "E0114 09:15:11.789456 1 scheduler.go:900] timed out waiting for caches to sync"
- curl to webhook endpoint: "POST /validate-node" average 324ms p95 at 09:14
- etcd follower log: "WARN raft: heartbeat ignored: no leader" around 09:13

If anyone else is adding notes: drop them here. Will synthesize into a clean postmortem once follow-ups done.

-- Ethan
